specStatements.text: When an ionic compound is melted or dissolved in water, the ions are free to move about within the liquid or solution. These liquids and solutions are able to conduct electricity and are called electrolytes.

Passing an electric current through electrolytes causes the ions to move to the electrodes. Positively charged ions move to the negative electrode (the cathode), and negatively charged ions move to the positive electrode (the anode). Ions are discharged at the electrodes producing elements. This process is called electrolysis.

(HT only) Throughout Section 4.4.3 Higher Tier students should be able to write half equations for the reactions occurring at the electrodes during electrolysis, and may be required to complete and balance supplied half equations.

When a simple ionic compound (eg lead bromide) is electrolysed in the molten state using inert electrodes, the metal (lead) is produced at the cathode and the non-metal (bromine) is produced at the anode.
Students should be able to predict the products of the electrolysis of binary ionic compounds in the molten state.

Metals can be extracted from molten compounds using electrolysis. Electrolysis is used if the metal is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon or if the metal reacts with carbon. Large amounts of energy are used in the extraction process to melt the compounds and to produce the electrical current.
Aluminium is manufactured by the electrolysis of a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite using carbon as the positive electrode (anode).
explain why a mixture is used as the electrolyte
explain why the positive electrode must be continually replaced.
The ions discharged when an aqueous solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes depend on the relative reactivity of the elements involved.
At the negative electrode (cathode), hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.
At the positive electrode (anode), oxygen is produced unless the solution contains halide ions when the halogen is produced.
This happens because in the aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions that are discharged.
Required practical 3: investigate what happens when aqueous solutions are electrolysed using inert electrodes. This should be an investigation involving developing a hypothesis.
During electrolysis, at the cathode (negative electrode), positively charged ions gain electrons and so the reactions are reductions.
At the anode (positive electrode), negatively charged ions lose electrons and so the reactions are oxidations.
Reactions at electrodes can be represented by half equations, for example:
2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
and
4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂ O + 4e⁻
or
4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂ O

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) Throughout Section 4.4.3 Higher Tier students should be able to write half equations for the reactions occurring at the electrodes during electrolysis
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every half equation in this content - concepts c10, c24, c25, c26 and c27, misconceptions m20 to m23, and questions q22 to q30 - is tagged tier "higher". No Foundation-tier item asks a student to write, complete or interpret a half equation; Foundation items ask only which element is produced at which electrode.

scopeNotes.statement: predict the products of the electrolysis of binary ionic compounds in the molten state
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Prediction questions for the molten state (q08, q09) use only binary compounds - two elements, one metal and one non-metal (magnesium chloride, potassium iodide, lead bromide). No molten compound containing a polyatomic ion is used for prediction, and molten-state prediction is kept separate from the aqueous rules of 4.4.3.4.

Every electrolysis described here, molten and aqueous, uses inert electrodes such as graphite or platinum (concept c07). Electrolysis with reactive electrodes - electroplating and the purification of copper - is not taught, since 4.4.3 does not include it.

scopeNotes.statement: using carbon as the positive electrode (anode)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The aluminium content is limited to what the specification states: a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite, carbon as the positive electrode, why the mixture is used, and why that electrode is replaced. No cell voltages, currents, yields or industrial plant details are introduced.

concepts.definition: An ionic compound that has been melted or dissolved in water, so that its ions are free to move about within the liquid or solution. Electrolytes are able to conduct electricity.

In a solid ionic compound the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice, so the solid cannot conduct. Melting the compound, or dissolving it in water, lets the ions move about, and it is this movement of ions that carries the current.
The process in which passing an electric current through an electrolyte causes the ions to move to the electrodes, where they are discharged, producing elements.
The negative electrode. Positively charged ions move to the cathode.
The positive electrode. Negatively charged ions move to the anode.
An ion is discharged when it loses its charge at an electrode, becoming a neutral atom or molecule of an element. The products of electrolysis are therefore always elements.
An electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that does not react with the electrolyte or with the products made during electrolysis.
When lead bromide is electrolysed in the molten state using inert electrodes, the metal, lead, is produced at the cathode and the non-metal, bromine, is produced at the anode: PbBr₂ → Pb + Br₂.

A compound made of just two elements, a metal and a non-metal. Electrolysed in the molten state, it always gives the metal at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode, so its products can be predicted from its name or formula.

An equation showing what happens to one kind of ion at one electrode, including the electrons gained or lost. The numbers of atoms and the total charge must balance on both sides, for example Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
Metals can be extracted from molten compounds using electrolysis. It is used if the metal is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon, or if the metal reacts with carbon.
Large amounts of energy are used in the extraction process, both to melt the compounds and to produce the electrical current. This is why extraction by electrolysis is expensive.

Aluminium is manufactured by the electrolysis of a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite, using carbon as the positive electrode (anode). Aluminium forms at the negative electrode and oxygen at the positive electrode.

concepts.term: Why a mixture is used as the electrolyte
concepts.definition: Aluminium oxide alone has a very high melting point. Mixing it with cryolite gives an electrolyte that melts at a much lower temperature, so less energy is needed to keep it molten and the process costs less.

concepts.term: Why the positive electrode is replaced
concepts.definition: Oxygen is produced at the positive electrode. At the high temperature of the cell it reacts with the carbon of the electrode to form carbon dioxide, so the carbon is worn away and the electrodes must be replaced continually.
The ions discharged when an aqueous solution is electrolysed using inert electrodes depend on the relative reactivity of the elements involved, not simply on which compound was dissolved.

concepts.term: Product at the cathode in solution
concepts.definition: At the negative electrode (cathode), hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen. If the metal is less reactive than hydrogen, such as copper, the metal itself is produced.

concepts.term: Product at the anode in solution
concepts.definition: At the positive electrode (anode), oxygen is produced unless the solution contains halide ions, when the halogen is produced instead.

In an aqueous solution, water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions. These ions are present as well as the ions of the dissolved compound, and it is they that are discharged when hydrogen or oxygen is the product.

An investigation of what happens when aqueous solutions are electrolysed using inert electrodes. A hypothesis is developed - for example about which solutions give a metal rather than hydrogen at the cathode - and then tested by identifying the products at each electrode.

concepts.term: Identifying the products in Required practical 3
concepts.definition: Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lighted splint is held to it; oxygen relights a glowing splint; chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper; a metal appears as a coating on the negative electrode.
During electrolysis, at the cathode (negative electrode), positively charged ions gain electrons and so the reactions are reductions.
At the anode (positive electrode), negatively charged ions lose electrons and so the reactions are oxidations.
Hydrogen ions are reduced at the cathode: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂. Two hydrogen ions and two electrons are needed because hydrogen gas exists as H₂ molecules and the charges must balance.
Hydroxide ions are oxidised at the anode: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻. Water appears as a product because the four hydroxide ions supply four hydrogen atoms that are not used in the oxygen molecule.

concepts.term: Two ways of writing an oxidation half equation
concepts.definition: The same anode reaction may be written with the electrons shown as a product or subtracted from the reactants: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ or 4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O. Both forms describe hydroxide ions losing four electrons.

concepts.term: A pair of electrode half equations
concepts.definition: Each electrolysis is described by two half equations: a reduction at the cathode and an oxidation at the anode. The specification gives 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ as the cathode example and 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ as the anode example.

misconceptions.question: Does solid lead bromide conduct electricity?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only when it is melted, or dissolved, can it conduct.
misconceptions.misconception: Ionic compounds are made of charged ions, so they must conduct electricity whether they are solid or molten.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that ionic compounds contain charged particles and conclude that charge alone is enough for conduction, without asking whether the charges can move.
misconceptions.correction: Conduction needs charges that are free to move. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice; only when the compound is melted or dissolved are the ions free to move about, which is why melted and dissolved ionic compounds are the electrolytes.

misconceptions.question: Where do the ions in molten lead bromide come from?
misconceptions.correct: They are already present in the solid; melting simply frees them to move.
misconceptions.misconception: Melting the compound splits the neutral atoms up and turns them into ions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word "electrolyte" is met at the same time as ion formation by electron transfer, so melting gets confused with the reaction that made the compound.
misconceptions.correction: An ionic solid is already built from ions held in a regular lattice. Melting or dissolving does not create the charges - it only breaks up the lattice so the ions can move about within the liquid or solution.

misconceptions.question: Which electrode do positively charged ions move to?
misconceptions.correct: The negative electrode, which is called the cathode.
misconceptions.misconception: The cathode must be the positive electrode, because positive ions are called cations and they go to the cathode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The names cathode and cation both begin with the same letters, so students assume they carry the same charge instead of remembering that opposite charges attract.
misconceptions.correction: Positively charged ions move to the negative electrode (the cathode) and negatively charged ions move to the positive electrode (the anode). The cathode is negative; it attracts positive ions precisely because it is opposite in charge.

misconceptions.question: What carries the current through the electrolyte itself?
misconceptions.correct: The moving ions carry the current through the liquid or solution.
misconceptions.misconception: Electrons flow through the electrolyte in the same way that they flow through the wires.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electric current is first taught as a flow of electrons in metal wires, and that single picture is then applied to every part of the circuit.
misconceptions.correction: In the wires and electrodes the current is carried by electrons, but inside the electrolyte it is carried by ions moving to the electrodes. Electrons are only transferred at the electrode surfaces, where the ions are discharged.

misconceptions.question: Do negatively charged ions move towards the negative electrode?
misconceptions.correct: No. They move to the positive electrode, the anode.
misconceptions.misconception: Negative ions are attracted to the negative electrode because both of them are negative.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Under time pressure students match like with like - "negative goes to negative" - instead of applying the rule that opposite charges attract.
misconceptions.correction: Negatively charged ions move to the positive electrode (the anode); positively charged ions move to the negative electrode (the cathode). Like charges repel, so a negative electrode pushes negative ions away.

misconceptions.question: What is the product at the anode when molten lead bromide is electrolysed?
misconceptions.correct: Bromine, which is formed as Br₂ molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: The product is bromide, Br⁻, because that is the ion that moves to the anode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students track the ion to the electrode and then name the product after the ion, forgetting that the ion is discharged there.
misconceptions.correction: Ions are discharged at the electrodes producing elements. Bromide ions lose their charge and pair up, so the element bromine, Br₂, is produced. The product of electrolysis is never an ion.

misconceptions.question: Is hydrogen produced when molten potassium iodide is electrolysed?
misconceptions.correct: No. Potassium is produced at the cathode and iodine at the anode.
misconceptions.misconception: Reactive metals like potassium can never be produced, so hydrogen is given off at the cathode instead.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reactivity rule for aqueous solutions is learned as a general rule and then applied to molten compounds as well.
misconceptions.correction: The reactivity rule only applies to aqueous solutions, where water provides hydrogen ions. A molten binary compound contains no water and no hydrogen ions, so the metal itself is produced at the cathode however reactive it is.

misconceptions.question: Are there water molecules present in a molten ionic compound?
misconceptions.correct: No. Molten means melted by heating, with no water present.
misconceptions.misconception: Molten and dissolved mean roughly the same thing, since both give a liquid that conducts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both states produce a conducting liquid with free ions, so the two words are treated as interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: A molten compound has been melted by heating and contains only its own ions. A solution contains water as well, and water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions. That difference is what changes the products.

misconceptions.question: Why is electrolysis used to extract aluminium?
misconceptions.correct: Because aluminium is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon.
misconceptions.misconception: Electrolysis is chosen because it is the cheaper and easier way of getting a metal out of its ore.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume industry always picks the cheapest method, so whichever method is used must be the cheapest one.
misconceptions.correction: Electrolysis is expensive: large amounts of energy are used to melt the compounds and to produce the electrical current. It is used only when reduction with carbon will not work, because the metal is too reactive or because it reacts with carbon.

misconceptions.question: Are all metals extracted from their compounds by electrolysis?
misconceptions.correct: No. Metals less reactive than carbon are extracted by reduction with carbon.
misconceptions.misconception: Electrolysis is the standard industrial way to get any metal out of its compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electrolysis is studied in detail and remembered vividly, so it becomes the default answer for every extraction question.
misconceptions.correction: Electrolysis is used if the metal is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon, or if the metal reacts with carbon. Metals below carbon in the reactivity series, such as iron, are obtained more cheaply by reduction with carbon.

misconceptions.question: What is the job of the cryolite in the aluminium cell?
misconceptions.correct: It lowers the melting point of the electrolyte, so less energy is needed.
misconceptions.misconception: Cryolite is a catalyst that speeds the electrolysis up without being used up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any added substance that is not obviously a reactant gets labelled a catalyst, because that is the only role students have a name for.
misconceptions.correction: Cryolite is not a catalyst. Aluminium oxide on its own melts at a very high temperature; mixing it with cryolite gives a molten mixture at a much lower temperature, which cuts the energy needed and so the cost.

misconceptions.question: Could aluminium oxide be dissolved in water instead of melted?
misconceptions.correct: No. In an aqueous solution hydrogen, not aluminium, would be produced.
misconceptions.misconception: Since dissolving also frees the ions, dissolving the oxide in water would be a much cheaper way to make aluminium.
misconceptions.whyItArises: "Melted or dissolved" is learned as one phrase, so the two routes look interchangeable and dissolving looks cheaper.
misconceptions.correction: Aluminium oxide is insoluble in water, and even if it dissolved, aluminium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen would be produced at the cathode. That is why a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite is used.

misconceptions.question: Why do the carbon anodes in the aluminium cell wear away?
misconceptions.correct: Oxygen made at the anode reacts with the hot carbon, forming carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.misconception: The anodes melt because the electrolyte around them is so hot.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The cell is obviously very hot and melting is the change students associate with heat, so melting is offered before any reaction is considered.
misconceptions.correction: The carbon is lost by reaction, not by melting. Oxygen is discharged at the positive electrode and at that temperature it reacts with the carbon to form carbon dioxide, so the electrode burns away and must be continually replaced.

misconceptions.question: Is the metal always produced at the cathode in an aqueous solution?
misconceptions.correct: No. Hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Metal ions are positive, so the metal must always be deposited at the negative electrode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The molten-state rule - metal at the cathode, non-metal at the anode - is applied to solutions without checking whether water changes the outcome.
misconceptions.correction: In an aqueous solution the water supplies hydrogen ions as well. At the cathode, hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen; the metal is deposited only when it is less reactive, as copper is.

misconceptions.question: What is produced at the cathode when sodium chloride solution is electrolysed?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen, because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Sodium metal is produced, because sodium ions are the positive ions in the solution.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students identify the positive ion in the dissolved salt and assume it must be the one discharged, forgetting the hydrogen ions from water.
misconceptions.correction: Both sodium ions and hydrogen ions move to the cathode, and the less reactive element is discharged. Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so hydrogen gas is produced and the sodium ions stay in the solution.

misconceptions.question: What gas forms at the anode when sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed?
misconceptions.correct: Oxygen, because the solution contains no halide ions.
misconceptions.misconception: The product at the anode always comes from the negative ion of the dissolved salt, so a sulfate gives a sulfur compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The halide rule is remembered as "the negative ion becomes the product", which then gets applied to every negative ion.
misconceptions.correction: At the anode, oxygen is produced unless the solution contains halide ions, when the halogen is produced. Sulfate is not a halide, so the hydroxide ions from water are discharged instead and oxygen is given off.

misconceptions.question: Where do the hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions in a solution come from?
misconceptions.correct: From water molecules, which break down producing H⁺ and OH⁻ ions.
misconceptions.misconception: They come from the dissolved ionic compound splitting up when it dissolves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Dissolving is taught as the compound separating into its ions, so every ion in the beaker is assumed to have come from that compound.
misconceptions.correction: The dissolved compound supplies only its own ions. In the aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions, and it is these that are discharged when hydrogen or oxygen is the product.

misconceptions.question: How can you show that the gas collected is oxygen?
misconceptions.correct: It relights a glowing splint.
misconceptions.misconception: Any gas that makes a splint react is hydrogen, so a squeaky pop is the test to try first.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The pop test is memorable and is met first, so it becomes the default test whenever a splint and a gas are involved.
misconceptions.correction: The two tests are different. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lighted splint is applied; oxygen relights a glowing splint. Chlorine is identified by bleaching damp litmus paper instead.

misconceptions.question: Why is the reaction at the cathode a reduction?
misconceptions.correct: Because the positively charged ions gain electrons there.
misconceptions.misconception: Reduction means losing electrons, since something that is reduced has lost something.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday meaning of "reduce" is to make smaller, which points to loss, and the OIL RIG rule is then recalled the wrong way round.
misconceptions.correction: Reduction is gain of electrons and oxidation is loss of electrons. At the cathode positively charged ions gain electrons, so those reactions are reductions; at the anode negatively charged ions lose electrons, so those reactions are oxidations.

misconceptions.question: Is 2H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂ an acceptable half equation?
misconceptions.correct: No. Two electrons are needed: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂.
misconceptions.misconception: A half equation only has to balance the atoms; the number of electrons can be left as one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing is first taught for ordinary equations, where only atoms are counted, so the electrons are treated as a label rather than a quantity.
misconceptions.correction: A half equation must balance for charge as well as atoms. Two H⁺ ions carry 2+ in total, so two electrons are needed to cancel that charge and give the neutral molecule H₂.

misconceptions.question: Why does water appear in the half equation 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻?
misconceptions.correct: The four hydroxide ions supply hydrogen atoms that must appear somewhere.
misconceptions.misconception: The anode reaction should just be 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻, since only oxygen is given off.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students balance the equation against what they can see bubbling off and forget that the hydrogen atoms in the hydroxide ions cannot vanish.
misconceptions.correction: Four OH⁻ ions contain four hydrogen and four oxygen atoms. Two oxygen atoms form O₂ and the rest form 2H₂O, so the equation is 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻, balanced for atoms and for charge.

misconceptions.question: Is 4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O a different reaction from 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are two ways of writing the same oxidation.
misconceptions.misconception: The minus sign means electrons are being added to the hydroxide ions on the left.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A minus sign is read as the arithmetic of the equation rather than as shorthand for electrons being taken away from the reactant.
misconceptions.correction: Subtracting electrons on the left and adding them on the right say the same thing: the hydroxide ions lose four electrons. Both forms are accepted for this oxidation at the anode.

misconceptions.question: What does it mean to say the electrodes are inert?
misconceptions.correct: They do not react with the electrolyte or with the products.
misconceptions.misconception: Inert just means the electrode is a good conductor that carries the current well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The only property of an electrode students have thought about is conduction, so any new word about electrodes is attached to that.
misconceptions.correction: Inert describes chemical behaviour, not conductivity. Graphite and platinum conduct but take no part in the reactions, so the products observed are due to the electrolyte alone.

misconceptions.question: What is reduced in the reaction at the cathode?
misconceptions.correct: The positive ions are reduced, because they gain electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Reduction means the mass of the electrode is reduced as the reaction goes on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word is taken in its everyday sense of getting smaller, and the electrode is the object in view, so the change is attached to the electrode.
misconceptions.correction: Reduction in chemistry means gain of electrons. At the cathode the positively charged ions gain electrons and become atoms; the cathode itself gains mass if a metal is deposited on it.

misconceptions.question: Is a copper wire an electrolyte?
misconceptions.correct: No. An electrolyte is a molten or dissolved ionic compound whose ions carry the current.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that conducts electricity is an electrolyte, so a metal wire counts as one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electrolytes are introduced as "liquids and solutions that conduct", and students shorten this to "things that conduct", dropping the requirement for mobile ions.
misconceptions.correction: An electrolyte is an ionic compound that is melted or dissolved in water, so that its ions are free to move. A metal conducts by means of delocalised electrons, contains no free ions and is not decomposed, so it is not an electrolyte.

misconceptions.question: A gas collected at the positive electrode relights a glowing splint. What is it?
misconceptions.correct: Oxygen. Only oxygen relights a glowing splint.
misconceptions.misconception: It is chlorine, because chlorine is the reactive gas that comes off at the positive electrode.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Chlorine is produced at the anode in the salt solutions used most often in class, so it is named for any gas collected there and then paired with whichever test comes to mind.
misconceptions.correction: Chlorine is identified by bleaching damp litmus paper, not by relighting a splint. Oxygen relights a glowing splint, and oxygen is the anode product unless the solution contains halide ions.

mcqs.stem: Solid lead bromide does not conduct electricity, but molten lead bromide does. Why?

options.text: Melting frees the ions so they can move about
options.rationale: Conduction needs charges that can move; melting breaks up the lattice and the ions become free to move within the liquid.

options.text: The solid contains no charged particles at all
options.rationale: A student who thinks charge alone causes conduction must explain the solid by denying it has any charges.

options.text: Melting turns the neutral atoms into free ions
options.rationale: Melting is confused with the electron transfer that formed the compound, so the ions seem to be made at this point.

options.text: Melting releases electrons that carry the current
options.rationale: Current in wires is carried by electrons, and that picture is transferred to the liquid instead of using moving ions.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is an electrolyte?

options.text: solid crystals of copper chloride
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think containing ions is enough, without asking whether the ions can move.

options.text: copper chloride dissolved in water
options.rationale: An ionic compound dissolved in water has free-moving ions, so the solution conducts and is an electrolyte.

options.text: a solution of sugar in water
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think dissolving anything in water produces free ions; sugar is molecular, so it does not.

options.text: a length of copper metal wire
options.rationale: Picked by students who equate electrolyte with anything that conducts electricity.

mcqs.stem: Molten zinc chloride is electrolysed. To which electrode do the chloride ions move, and why?

options.text: To the cathode, because both of them are negative
options.rationale: Like is matched with like instead of applying attraction between opposite charges.

options.text: To the anode, because that electrode is negative
options.rationale: The destination is right but the charge is wrong, which is what a student who has swapped the electrode names writes.

options.text: To the anode, because that electrode is positive
options.rationale: Negatively charged ions move to the positive electrode, the anode, because opposite charges attract.

options.text: To the cathode, because chloride ions are positive
options.rationale: Chosen by students who forget that the -ide ending marks a negative ion.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by saying that ions are discharged at an electrode?

options.text: They travel along the wires as an electric current
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the ions themselves move round the whole circuit.

options.text: They keep their charge but stick to the electrode
options.rationale: Students who name the product after the ion imagine the ion simply collecting there unchanged.

options.text: They swap places with ions of the opposite charge
options.rationale: A vague memory of ion exchange, plausible because ions of both signs are moving in the liquid.

options.text: They lose their charge and become atoms of an element
options.rationale: Discharge is the loss of charge at the electrode, and the products of electrolysis are elements.

mcqs.stem: Molten zinc chloride is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What happens to the zinc ions?

options.text: They move to the cathode and are discharged as zinc
options.rationale: Positively charged ions move to the negative electrode and are discharged there, producing the element.

options.text: They move to the anode because they are positive ions
options.rationale: Chosen when cation is matched to anode, or when the electrode names have been swapped.

options.text: They move to the cathode and stay as ions in the liquid
options.rationale: The movement is right but discharge is left out, so the ion never becomes an element.

options.text: They stay still while electrons move through the liquid
options.rationale: The metal-wire picture of current is applied to the electrolyte itself.

mcqs.stem: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What are the products?

options.text: bromine at the cathode and lead at the anode
options.rationale: The standard answer with the electrodes swapped, written by students unsure which electrode is negative.

options.text: lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode
options.rationale: The metal is produced at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode, as the specification states for lead bromide.

options.text: hydrogen at the cathode and bromine at the anode
options.rationale: The aqueous reactivity rule is applied to a molten compound that contains no water.

options.text: lead at the cathode and oxygen at the anode
options.rationale: Oxygen is assumed to come from water, which a student thinks is present in any liquid electrolyte.

mcqs.stem: The electrodes used to electrolyse molten lead bromide are described as inert. What does this mean?

options.text: They conduct the current better than any other material
options.rationale: Conduction is the only electrode property many students have considered, so any new term is attached to it.

options.text: They cannot be melted by the hot molten electrolyte
options.rationale: Heat is the obvious hazard in the experiment, so resisting melting sounds like the right kind of property.

options.text: They do not react with the electrolyte or the products
options.rationale: Inert describes chemical behaviour: the electrode takes no part in the reactions, so the products come from the electrolyte alone.

options.text: They are not connected directly to the power supply
options.rationale: Inert is read as inactive in the circuit rather than unreactive in chemistry.

mcqs.stem: Molten calcium bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which statement about the products is correct?

options.text: Hydrogen forms at the cathode, because calcium is a reactive metal
options.rationale: The reactivity rule for aqueous solutions is applied to a melt, which contains no hydrogen ions.

options.text: Oxygen forms at the anode, because water is present in the liquid
options.rationale: Molten and dissolved are treated as the same, so water is assumed to be in the melt.

options.text: Bromide ions gather at the anode, but they are not discharged
options.rationale: The ion is tracked to the electrode and then named as the product, with discharge left out.

options.text: Calcium forms at the cathode, even though it is a reactive metal
options.rationale: A molten binary ionic compound gives the metal at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode, whatever the reactivity of the metal.

mcqs.stem: Molten potassium iodide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Iodine forms at the anode because iodide ions are negative
options.rationale: Negatively charged iodide ions move to the positive electrode and are discharged as the element iodine.

options.text: Hydrogen forms at the cathode because potassium is reactive
options.rationale: The aqueous rule about reactive metals is used even though no water is present in a melt.

options.text: Iodine forms at the cathode because iodine is a non-metal
options.rationale: A student remembers that a non-metal is a product but guesses the electrode by elimination.

options.text: Potassium forms at the anode because metal ions are positive
options.rationale: The correct charge on the metal ion is paired with the wrong electrode name.

mcqs.stem: Why is aluminium extracted by electrolysis rather than by reduction with carbon?

options.text: Electrolysis is a cheaper method than heating with carbon
options.rationale: Students assume industry always uses the cheapest route, so the route used must be cheapest.

options.text: Aluminium is too reactive to be extracted using carbon
options.rationale: Electrolysis is used if the metal is too reactive to be extracted by reduction with carbon.

options.text: Electrolysis is the method used for extracting all metals
options.rationale: Electrolysis is studied in most detail, so it becomes the default extraction answer.

options.text: Aluminium oxide cannot be heated to a high temperature
options.rationale: A half-memory of the very high melting point of aluminium oxide, turned into the wrong reason.

mcqs.stem: Extracting a metal by electrolysis is expensive. Why?

options.text: The metal made has to be purified by reduction with carbon
options.rationale: The two extraction methods are muddled into one process rather than treated as alternatives.

options.text: The cryolite acts as a catalyst and is used up as it works
options.rationale: Follows directly from believing cryolite is a catalyst, with the added error that catalysts are consumed.

options.text: Energy is needed to melt the compound and make the current
options.rationale: The specification states that large amounts of energy are used both to melt the compounds and to produce the electrical current.

options.text: The electrodes are made from rare and costly pure metals
options.rationale: Plausible because inert electrodes include platinum, but the industrial anodes are carbon.

mcqs.stem: What is used as the electrolyte in the manufacture of aluminium?

options.text: a solution of aluminium oxide dissolved in water
options.rationale: "Melted or dissolved" is treated as interchangeable, and dissolving sounds cheaper.

options.text: molten aluminium oxide with no other substance
options.rationale: Chosen by students who see cryolite as an optional additive rather than part of the electrolyte.

options.text: molten cryolite with powdered carbon stirred in
options.rationale: Carbon is remembered as part of the cell, but it is the electrode, not part of the electrolyte.

options.text: a molten mixture of aluminium oxide and cryolite
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states, and the mixture melts far below the melting point of the oxide alone.

mcqs.stem: Why is cryolite mixed with the aluminium oxide?

options.text: It lowers the melting point, so less energy is needed
options.rationale: The mixture melts at a much lower temperature than aluminium oxide alone, cutting the energy used and the cost.

options.text: It is a catalyst, so the electrolysis happens faster
options.rationale: Any additive with no obvious role is labelled a catalyst, the one term students have for it.

options.text: It supplies the aluminium ions that form the metal
options.rationale: Plausible if cryolite is assumed to be the aluminium source, since its name is unfamiliar.

options.text: It stops the carbon anodes from burning away
options.rationale: Links the additive to the other well-known feature of the cell, the electrodes wearing away.

mcqs.stem: Why must the positive electrode in the aluminium cell be continually replaced?

options.text: The carbon electrode melts in the hot molten electrolyte
options.rationale: Heat is the obvious feature of the cell and melting is the change students link with heat.

options.text: Oxygen made there reacts with the hot carbon electrode
options.rationale: Oxygen is discharged at the anode and reacts with the carbon at that temperature to form carbon dioxide, wearing the electrode away.

options.text: Aluminium is deposited on it and has to be scraped off
options.rationale: Chosen when the electrodes are swapped, since aluminium does collect at the other electrode.

options.text: The cryolite slowly dissolves the carbon of the electrode
options.rationale: Cryolite is known to be a solvent for the oxide, so it is assumed to dissolve the anode too.

mcqs.stem: When an aqueous solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes, what decides which ions are discharged?

options.text: which ions the dissolved compound splits into
options.rationale: Only the ions from the salt are counted, so the ions from water are never considered.

options.text: which of the ions present is a metal ion
options.rationale: Follows from believing the metal is always deposited at the cathode.

options.text: the relative reactivity of the elements involved
options.rationale: The specification states that the ions discharged depend on the relative reactivity of the elements involved.

options.text: the size of the current passed through it
options.rationale: Current is the variable the student controls, so it feels like the thing that changes the products.

mcqs.stem: Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What is produced at the cathode, and why?

options.text: sodium, because the metal is always produced at the cathode
options.rationale: The molten-state rule is carried over to solutions without checking the reactivity.

options.text: sodium, because sodium ions are the positive ions present
options.rationale: Only the ions from the salt are considered, so sodium ions look like the only candidate.

options.text: oxygen, because water molecules break down at that electrode
options.rationale: Water is correctly identified as a source of ions but the wrong ion is sent to the cathode.

options.text: hydrogen, because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen
options.rationale: At the cathode hydrogen is produced if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, which sodium is.

mcqs.stem: Sodium sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What is given off at the anode?

options.text: oxygen, from the hydroxide ions in the water
options.rationale: Oxygen is produced at the anode unless the solution contains halide ions, and sulfate is not a halide.

options.text: sulfur dioxide, from the sulfate ions present
options.rationale: The halide rule is remembered as "the negative ion becomes the product" and applied to sulfate.

options.text: hydrogen, from the hydrogen ions in the water
options.rationale: The right source is chosen but the ion is sent to the wrong electrode.

options.text: no gas at all, as sulfate ions are unreactive
options.rationale: Sulfate is known to be a spectator ion in other reactions, so nothing is expected to happen.

mcqs.stem: Potassium bromide solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. What is produced at the anode?

options.text: oxygen, because oxygen always forms at this electrode
options.rationale: The rule is remembered without its exception, so oxygen is given every time.

options.text: bromine, because the solution contains halide ions
options.rationale: Oxygen forms at the anode unless halide ions are present, and bromide is a halide, so the halogen is produced.

options.text: hydrogen, because water breaks down at this electrode
options.rationale: Water is correctly seen as a source of ions but hydrogen is sent to the wrong electrode.

options.text: potassium, because it moves to the positive electrode
options.rationale: Chosen when the charges on the electrodes have been swapped.

mcqs.stem: In an aqueous solution, where do the hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions come from?

options.text: from the dissolved compound splitting
options.rationale: Dissolving is taught as separation into ions, so every ion present is credited to the salt.

options.text: from the electrodes releasing the ions
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the electrodes take a chemical part in the process.

options.text: from water molecules breaking down
options.rationale: The specification states that in the aqueous solution water molecules break down producing hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions.

options.text: from the current splitting the atoms
options.rationale: The current is seen as the agent that creates the ions rather than as what moves them.

mcqs.stem: In Required practical 3, a gas collects at the positive electrode. Which result shows that it is oxygen?

options.text: A lighted splint burns with a squeaky pop
options.rationale: The pop test is met first and is used as the default whenever a splint and a gas appear.

options.text: Damp litmus paper is bleached white by it
options.rationale: Students who expect chlorine at every positive electrode reach for the chlorine test.

options.text: Limewater turns milky when it is shaken
options.rationale: A well-known gas test, chosen when tests are recalled without matching them to gases.

options.text: A glowing splint is relit by the gas
options.rationale: Relighting a glowing splint is the test for oxygen.

mcqs.stem: A student electrolyses several solutions with inert electrodes. Which hypothesis could this investigation test?

options.text: A metal forms at the cathode only if it is less reactive than hydrogen
options.rationale: This is a testable prediction: choose salts of metals above and below hydrogen and see which give a metal coating.

options.text: The metal in the dissolved compound always forms at the cathode
options.rationale: Testable, but it is the molten-state rule wrongly carried across to solutions.

options.text: The gas formed at the anode always comes from the dissolved salt
options.rationale: Follows from thinking the negative ion of the salt is always the anode product.

options.text: Every gas made in electrolysis can be identified by the pop test
options.rationale: Chosen by students who treat the pop test as the general test for a gas.

mcqs.stem: Why are the reactions at the cathode described as reductions?

options.text: Positively charged ions lose electrons there
options.rationale: OIL RIG recalled the wrong way round, so reduction is taken to mean loss.

options.text: Positively charged ions gain electrons there
options.rationale: Reduction is gain of electrons, and at the cathode the positive ions gain the electrons supplied.

options.text: The mass of the cathode is reduced as it runs
options.rationale: The everyday sense of reduce, made smaller, is applied to the electrode.

options.text: Oxygen is removed from the ions at that electrode
options.rationale: Reduction as loss of oxygen is a real definition, but there is no oxygen in these ions to remove.

mcqs.stem: Copper chloride solution is electrolysed. Which statement about the anode reaction is correct?

options.text: Chloride ions are reduced because they lose electrons
options.rationale: The electron movement is right but the term is swapped, the classic OIL RIG slip.

options.text: Chloride ions are oxidised because they gain electrons
options.rationale: The term is right but justified by the wrong electron movement, showing the rule is not held together.

options.text: Chloride ions are oxidised because they lose electrons
options.rationale: At the anode negatively charged ions lose electrons, and loss of electrons is oxidation.

options.text: Copper ions are oxidised because they lose electrons
options.rationale: The positive ion is sent to the positive electrode, so the wrong species is oxidised.

mcqs.stem: Copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which half equation shows the cathode reaction?

options.text: Cu²⁺ → Cu + 2e⁻
options.rationale: Electrons put on the product side, which describes loss of electrons and so oxidation.

options.text: Cu²⁺ + e⁻ → Cu
options.rationale: Atoms balance but the charge does not; only the electron count has been overlooked.

options.text: Cu + 2e⁻ → Cu²⁺
options.rationale: Written backwards by a student who reads the equation as copper turning into its ion.

options.text: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu
options.rationale: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so copper ions gain two electrons and are reduced to copper metal.

mcqs.stem: Which half equation for the production of hydrogen at the cathode is correct?

options.text: 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂
options.rationale: This is the equation given in the specification: two hydrogen ions gain two electrons to form one hydrogen molecule.

options.text: 2H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂
options.rationale: Atoms balance but the charge does not, because only the electrons have been left unbalanced.

options.text: 2H⁺ – 2e⁻ → H₂
options.rationale: Shows electrons being lost at the cathode, the reverse of reduction.

options.text: H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻
options.rationale: The correct oxidation of hydrogen, chosen by a student who does not check the direction.

mcqs.stem: Dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which pair of half equations is correct?

options.text: cathode 2H⁺ – 2e⁻ → H₂; anode 4OH⁻ + 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O
options.rationale: Both equations have the electrons on the wrong side, the consequence of swapping oxidation and reduction.

options.text: cathode 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂; anode 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
options.rationale: A reduction at the cathode and an oxidation at the anode, exactly as the specification gives them.

options.text: cathode 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂; anode 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻
options.rationale: The water is left out, so the hydrogen atoms from the hydroxide ions simply disappear.

options.text: cathode H⁺ + e⁻ → H₂; anode 2OH⁻ → O₂ + H₂O + 2e⁻
options.rationale: Halved throughout without checking, leaving both equations unbalanced for atoms.

mcqs.stem: Which half equation correctly shows oxygen being produced at the anode?

options.text: 4OH⁻ + 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O
options.rationale: Electrons on the left make it a reduction, which cannot happen at the anode.

options.text: 2OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 2e⁻
options.rationale: The coefficients are halved unevenly, so the atoms no longer balance.

options.text: 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻
options.rationale: Balanced for atoms and charge, and the form given in the specification.

options.text: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻
options.rationale: The reverse reaction, picked by a student who checks only that it balances.

mcqs.stem: The anode reaction can be written 4OH⁻ – 4e⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O. Which statement about this is correct?

options.text: It is a different reaction in which the ions gain four electrons
options.rationale: The minus sign is read as arithmetic on the equation instead of as electron loss.

options.text: It is the cathode reaction rather than the anode reaction shown
options.rationale: Chosen when electrons on the left are automatically taken to mean reduction.

options.text: It is an unbalanced version that would not be accepted by AQA
options.rationale: The unfamiliar minus sign looks like a mistake to a student who has only met one form.

options.text: It is the same reaction, with the electrons lost shown on the left
options.rationale: Subtracting electrons from the reactants and adding them to the products both describe loss of four electrons.

mcqs.stem: Molten aluminium oxide is electrolysed. Which half equation for the anode is correctly balanced?

options.text: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻
options.rationale: Two oxide ions carry 4- in total, so four electrons are lost as they form one oxygen molecule.

options.text: 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 2e⁻
options.rationale: The electrons are counted per ion rather than in total, so the charge does not balance.

options.text: 2O²⁻ + 4e⁻ → O₂
options.rationale: Electrons gained rather than lost, which would be a reduction and cannot occur at the anode.

options.text: O²⁻ → O₂ + 2e⁻
options.rationale: The charge balances but the oxygen atoms do not, since O₂ needs two oxide ions.

mcqs.stem: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed. Which half equation shows what happens at the anode?

options.text: 2Br⁻ → 2Br + 2e⁻
options.rationale: The product is written as separate atoms because the student names the element without its molecular formula.

options.text: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
options.rationale: Two bromide ions each lose an electron and join to form a bromine molecule, balanced for atoms and charge.

options.text: 2Br⁻ + 2e⁻ → Br₂
options.rationale: Electrons gained rather than lost, the reduction written where an oxidation belongs.

options.text: Br₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Br⁻
options.rationale: The reverse reaction, chosen by a student who checks the balancing but not the direction.
